The work and the approach
  

   

  What I do
  
     I work at the intersection of public data and policy decisions,taking 
        administrative and fiscal data that governments produce but rarely 
        interrogate and turning them into evidence that decision-makers can 
        act on.
    
      My focus is Nepal's intergovernmental fiscal system: how federal 
      resources flow to provincial and local governments, whether that flow 
      reflects stated policy priorities, and where the gaps between allocation 
      logic and actual outcomes are widest. I work across health, education, 
      agricultural policy which is part of the same fiscal architecture that shapes each of these verticles.
    
  
  

  How I work
  
     
      All analysis is produced in R and published as reproducible Quarto 
      documents. I work directly from primary sources, such as those from Ministry of Finance's budget data, conditional grant records from various ministries and government entities, and household survey microdata, rather than aggregated 
      secondary sources.
      
    
      I am especially interested in subnational variation: the patterns that 
      disappear when data is aggregated to the national level. Nepal's 
      federal system creates 753 units of observation. Most analysis uses 
      seven provinces. The most important findings tend to live in the 
      difference between those two scales.
    
  

  Background
  
    
      I am based in Kathmandu. My work on Nepal's fiscal decentralisation 
      has covered health workforce financing, basic education conditional 
      grants, out-of-pocket health expenditure, and electoral constituency 
      analysis. Earlier work includes trade policy involving
      Nepal's sugarcane sector and Nepal's trade landscape.
    
    
      I am available for consulting engagements, research collaborations, 
      and analytical commissions. If your organisation needs someone who 
      can move between government budget documents and actionable 
      policy recommendations, and produce the analysis in between, 
      I would be glad to talk.

Gandaki Province receives 12.21% of the total budget allocated under Budget Subhead 3700102, despite comprising only 8.42% of the total population. It would be interesting to explore whether there is a correlation between budget allocation and performance in various health indicators across provinces. For instance, how does Gandaki—where per capita budget allocation is high—compare to Bagmati, which has a lower per capita budget allocation relative to other provinces?
It is important to note that Budget Subhead No. 3700102 covers health-related human resource costs at the local level. Ideally, the budget allocation should be proportional to the actual size of the health workforce in each local unit. Assuming a direct proportional relationship between budget allocation and the number of health workers, Gandaki and Karnali provinces would have the highest number of per capita health workers at the local level. Therefore, analyzing the relationship between per capita spending on local-level health workers and actual health outcomes would be a valuable exercise in optimizing government spending and improving efficiency at the outcome level.

Equity Analysis
Lets make an attempt to evaluate whether the budget allocation is proportional to population size across local level governments in Nepal.








Figure 7: Simple Linear Model of Population and total budget allocation for each local level





Figure 7 attempts to visualize the relationship between population (in 1000s) and total budget allocation (in 10 million). A linear regression line with a confidence interval is included to show the general trend between population size and budget allocation.
Following are the key observations based on the chart:

Positive Correlation: There is a weak positive correlation between population and budget allocation, as indicated by the regression line.
The low R² value: the low R² value (0.11) suggests that population alone does not strongly explain budget allocation. Only 11% of the variation in the budget is explained by population alone. Other factors (eg policy decisions, political considerations) could be at play.
The Curious Case of Six Metros: Pokhara, Birgunj and Bharatpur received higher budget than predicted by the linear model based on the population size. Similarly, Lalitpur, Biratnagar and Kathmandu received significantly low amount of budget than prediction. This too further substantiates that (in this case Metros) population alone is not the main driver of budget allocation.
Explaining Linear Model and Coefficient The regression equation shown in the plot is:\[y = 2.43 \times 10^{+7} + 80.5x\]
The intercept \[\beta_o = 2.43  \times  10^{+7}\] represents the value of Total Budget if the population is zero. In this context we can presume that this value (24.3 million) is the bare minimum cost estimate for human resources regardless of the population.
The slope \[\beta_1 = 80.5\] means for every additional 1000 people, the total budget increases by 80.5 million (or 8.05 Crores)

Lets see if there are any Patterns at Provinces








Figure 8: Linear Model (Total Budget V Population) at each local level for each provinces





Figure 8 illustrates relationship between total budget allocated and population along with a simple linear model for each provinces. Following observations can be made:

In Gandaki and Madhesh Province, the R² is significantly higher (at 0.52) than other Provinces. This implies that there is moderately strong positive correlation between population and total budget allocated in these Provinces. This also means that 52% of variance in budget allocation can be explained by the population.
In Koshi and Sudur Paschim, the R² value is < 0.01, this means population cannot be considered a predictor for total budget allocation.

text:
Key Takeaways

The primary health service (ie प्राथमिक स्वास्थ्य सेवा) comprises the highest budgetary allocation (20.64 billion) among conditional grant (under fiscal transfer) provided which provided to Local Level for health related expenses. The government guideline makes it clear that the expenses under this heading is related to salary and allowances for the human resources working at the heath facilities at local level. The data exercise makes it very clear that budgetary allocation under this subheading is not strong function of population
Subnational level health indicator (LG level) could be used to evaluate the efficiency of budgetary allocation.
The policy questions :

The data suggests that there is a high variations in the number of health personnel employed at local level (everything remaining constant, budget volume is fundamentally a function of number of health personnel). What determines the number of health personnel at local level? Should the population it caters to be a general predictor of the number of health personnel and vis-à-vis total budget allocation?
What other variables, other than population, should determine the budgetary allocation (or number of health personnel) at Local Level? Or is it such that the local levels with lower per capita budgetary allocation are “healthy patches of population” that ought to require less investment from the state ?

title: Financing Basic Education- From a lens of student-teacher ratio
text:
This exercise is an attempt to analyse conditional grants as allocated by the Federal Government of Nepal for education at Local Level. Pursuant to the constitution of Nepal, the basic education falls within the power of the Local Level Governments.
The legacy of pre-federal education system still holds a strong grip in the Education Sector in Nepal including those in the Local Level - which have constitutional power of Basic Education. This means, the federal government have had hands-on approach in matters of resource allocation for the publicly funded school at local level, via conditional grants. The conditional grants for education targeted at publicly funded schools at local level comprises a significant chunk of total government spending for any single program.
While there exists significant and acute [horizontal] fiscal imbalance among local level governments to run and operate their constitutional mandate of basic education, which makes it only imperative for federal government to intervene and correct the imbalance. However, the modus operandi of federal government of Nepal in allocating resources to counter the pervasive fiscal imbalance in Education Sector in Local Level has not been within the spirit of constitutional mandate. In practice public education system is being run as a federal program; for example, in the Fiscal Year 2080-81, the federal budget had 18 different activity code amounting to 135 billion rupees for 753 Local Level Government under conditional grants for education. The level of micro-management in resource allocation of education sector is not only against the spirit of constitution and federalism, it also adds administrative cost to federal government.
This exercise makes an attempt to analyse data on budget and school to understand budgetary allocation under conditional grant from federal government to local government which could be used to identify possible alternative methods to decentralize the process such that Local Level government are empowered to exercise their constitutional power of basic education.

title: Who’s Really Competing? A Screening Approach to Contractor Concentration in Nepal’s Public Procurement
text:
The design of competitive public procurement works when many qualified suppliers compete for government contracts. When a small number of contractors win most of the value at a given public entity, such concentration is worth a closer look; among other things it can signal a genuinely thin supplier market, or it can signal something narrower such as specification, timelines, or processes that quietly favour a few suppliers.
This brief attempts to make use of one screening method, the the Effective Contractor Count (ECC) derived from the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, to systematically identify public entities participating in Nepal’s e-Government Procurement (e-GP) system that show unusually concentrated contractor bases, using award data from April 26, 2013 to July 30, 2026. The goal of the exercise is not to diagnose potential corruption or any wrong doing but to make a case for a method to identify and shortlist cases where concentration is high enough, and unexplained, to justify further oversight and scrutiny by concerned authorities.

title: Who’s Really Competing? A Screening Approach to Contractor Concentration in Nepal’s Public Procurement
text:
Measuring Contractor Concentration: The HHI
To measure how concentrated a public entity’s contractor base is, this exercise uses the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard tool that regulators around the globe use to assess market concentration. HHI is calculated by taking each contractor’s share of any entity’s total contract value, squaring it, and summing across all contractors. The result ranges from near-zero (spending by the entity spread evenly across many contractors) to 10,000 (a single contractor captures everything).
HHI score, ranging from near-zero to 10,000, is not intuitive enough and for this reason, this exercise converts it into the Effective Contractor Count (ECC). ECC is the number of equally-sized contractors that would produce the same HHI score. So, ECC value of 8 would mean that an entity’s spending is about as concentrated as if it were split evenly among 8 contractors, even if, on paper, twenty contractors won at least one contract in that particular entity. This makes concentration comparable across entities of very different sizes, and easier to reason about than an abstract index score. ECC is calculated as the inverse of the HHI (the sum of each contractor’s squared value share at each public entity).
It is to be noted that ECC should be read as a screening indicator and not a verdict of any wrongdoing. A low ECC could genuinely reflect a thin supplier market because of nature of the market or works or services rather than any irregularity in how contracts were awarded. This exercise treats a low ECC as the start of a question, and not the end of one.

The ECC across Public Entities
Figure 3 below plots each public entity’s effective contractor count (ECC) against its number of contracts (in log scale), with bubble size showing total procurement value. A clear general pattern emerges in the plot; the entities with more awards tend to also have higher ECC, which, makes intuitive sense as more transactions create more opportunities for different contractors to win work. However, this otherwise linear relationship doesn’t always hold which is worth noting.
The entities that depart from the general pattern at higher contract volumes are of interest. One entity in particular in the plot stands out which accounts for the largest bubble on the chart yet sits at a comparatively modest ECC given the number of awards it has issued. In other words, its spending is concentrated among relatively few contractors despite substantial transaction volume and total value, which is a very different scenario from an entity with few contracts and low ECC simply because it hasn’t transacted enough for competition to emerge.
By contrast, some entities with moderate-to-high contract counts show notably higher ECC than others, at similar volumes indicating, comparatively broad-based competition for entities of similar size and activity.








Figure 3: Bubble chart illustrating ECC values and number of contract for public entities







The threshold for screening
On minimum contract threshold. Public Entities with few awards issued almost always show low ECC, whether or not real concentration is an issue. There is simply not enough activity to tell the difference. Figure 4 shows this pattern holds roughly around the 20 contracts point which also happens to be the third quartile (see Table 2) of the public entity in this dataset. This exercise, therefore, limits its screening (for contractor concentration) to the public entities with at least 20 awards issued, which accounts for 25% of total entities in the dataset.








Figure 4: Entities with few awards looks to have similar ECC





On maximum ECC threshold. A two cluster split (k-means) was applied to the entities with sufficient award history (ie total award count above 20). Figure 5 shows the result, a clear boundary emerges around ECC approximately at 5.8, splitting entities with a boundary landing in a visibly empty stretch of the distribution, rather than cutting through a cluster. It is therefore this exercise adopts ECC < 5.5 as its screening threshold.
A combination of minimum of total awards at 20 and maximum of ECC at 5.5 identifies 8 entities for closer examination.

title: Who’s Really Competing? A Screening Approach to Contractor Concentration in Nepal’s Public Procurement
text:
Recommendations
This screening exercise was designed to narrow 183 public entities down to a small number of cases warranting closer attention. This by no means is an attempt to diagnose corruption or irregularity or any wrongdoing, which award-level data alone cannot establish. The exercise has led to three directions worth noting:

Prioritize entity-level review, starting with the evident cases. Road Infrastructure Development Office, Kapilvastu and Infrastructure Development Office, Solukhumbu stand out even within the flagged group. Both show a pattern where a single contractor seems to have secured over three-quarters of total contract value, despite (in Kapilvastu’s case) a large nominal pool of 53 contractors. Oversight bodies who are often plagued with limited audit capacity could use this kind of screening method to prioritize which entities to examine first, rather than reviewing entities at random or by size alone.
Identifying a process-level concentration before intervening. Not all public entities with low ECC value calls for same response. For example Krishi Samagri Company Limited’s concentration is plausibly explained by the nature of goods procured ie fertilizer through foreign companies. It is fundamentally different from the concentration observed in case of Kapilvastu. Hence, no same fix would apply to both. For example, unbundling contracts to attract more bidders and more contractors would likely help in Kapilvasut’s case but would do little to nothing for Krishi Samagri Company Limited. Any remedial response should be matched to the patterns each public entities actually exhibit.
Limits of award-level data. Every awards observed and analysed in this exercise was procured through NCB, yet the outcomes ranged from near-total single contractor dominated scenario to more distributed competition. Hence, the dataset clearly has its limitation. A bidding-stage data would substantially improve any screening exercise like this.

Indicator II : Margin of Victory (MoV)
Concept
MoV reflects competitiveness. It is calcuated as a differece (in percentage point of vote share) between the winner and runner-up (rank 1 and 2).
Smaller MoV -> Higher chances of contestability or voters are tightly divided
Larger MoV -> Strong dominance by a single party or voters significantly more inclined towards a dominant party.
Strategic Value

The federal MoV, at prime facie, a measure how tightly the constituency is contested with. Lower MoV value is a favourable condition, at large, for the new entrants
Identify segments of wards or invidiual wards with similar traits to formulate similar plans :

For example in wards with Lower MoV: Higher chances of contestability
In case of ward with higher MoV: suggests strong dominance by a single party and hence the startegy could be combination of anti-incumbency agendas along with other relevant measures based on the dominant party.

Concept
ILV measures how much voter preference fluctuates within a ward across elections.

ILV is a measure of spread of MoV values within each ward. Generally, higher ILV (higher flactuation) provides strategic advantage for new political options as voters have not consolidated to any political force.
